issue: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1152, must the government plead and prove a defendant's non-Indian status as an element of the offense, or is Indian status an affirmative defense that the defendant must first raise?

sides.position: Non-Indian status is an element of the § 1152 offense that the government must allege and prove at trial.
cases: United States v. Prentiss, 256 F.3d 971 (10th Cir. 2001) (en banc)
United States v. Ruiz, No. 24-2128 (10th Cir. Jan. 12, 2026)

sides.position: Indian or non-Indian status is an affirmative defense: the defendant must first properly raise it, and the government bears the ultimate burden of proof only once it is raised.
cases: United States v. Hester, 719 F.2d 1040 (9th Cir. 1983)
United States v. Haggerty, 997 F.3d 292 (5th Cir. 2021)

this_court: Tenth Circuit treats non-Indian status as an element under Prentiss and declines to depart from it, but urges en banc reconsideration
quote: Circuits have split on the question whether the Indian or non-Indian status of the defendant must be pleaded and proved by the government in a prosecution under 18 U.S.C.A. § 1152.
cite: United States v. Ruiz, No. 24-2128 (10th Cir. 2026)
